opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say I categorically favor one over the other. Both are forms of test-time adaptation, and that's the key shift. For years the dominant paradigm was: train a big model, freeze it, then query it at inference. That's static inference. It's essentially fetching and reapplying memorized patterns, and it breaks down when you face something genuinely novel. Both test-time training and the o1 approach move away from that, and that's why they do much better on benchmarks like ARC.

But they adapt in very different ways. Test-time training adapts parametrically: you take the few demonstration examples, maybe augment them, and fine-tune the weights on them. You're still doing curve fitting, just locally and on the fly. That works surprisingly well, but you're still constrained by gradient descent: you need a decent number of examples, the result is a continuous interpolative function, and it doesn't really give you discrete, compositional reasoning.

What o1 appears to do is closer to search. It explores the space of possible chains of thought and evaluates which branches lead somewhere useful. You can think of a chain of thought as a kind of natural-language program. So o1 is doing something like program synthesis: searching over a space of recombinations of the knowledge and skills the model already has, assembling a new solution for the problem at hand. That's much closer to what I think intelligence actually is: taking your existing building blocks and recombining them on the fly into a new model of the situation, from very little data.

So the reason I find that direction more promising in principle is that search over discrete, compositional structures can generalize far more strongly than fitting a continuous function to a handful of examples. Gradient descent is great for perception and intuition, for what you might call type-one thinking. But for novel reasoning, for type-two thinking, you need some form of discrete search.

That said, I don't think o1 is the endgame either. Its search is still guided by, and limited to, what's in the model's latent space. Its chain-of-thought "programs" are expressed in natural language, which is a fairly inefficient program representation. I think the systems that eventually crack this will merge the two: deep learning to provide intuition, to tell you which branches of the search space are worth exploring, and explicit discrete program search to do the actual composition and verification. Deep learning and program synthesis aren't competitors; they're complements.

r003.rationale: It calls a chain of thought a natural-language program, but does not clearly say it is a program for the model to execute.

r006.rationale: It does not characterize human knowledge recombination as functional composition or compare it with gradient descent.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I don't think I favor one over the other in absolute terms. I think they're both instances of the same fundamental idea, which is that you need to do some form of search or adaptation at inference time if you want to handle genuinely novel problems. A fixed, static model that just does one forward pass is never going to generalize to something it hasn't seen, because all it can do is fetch and recombine patterns it memorized during training.

So the question is really about what kind of adaptation you're doing. Test-time training, the way people have applied it to ARC for instance, works by fine-tuning the weights of the model on the demonstration pairs of the specific task you're looking at. That's quite effective, and it's a real form of adaptation. But it's a somewhat blunt instrument. You're doing gradient descent on the entire parameter space to fit a handful of examples, and you're essentially overwriting the model for each task. It's expensive, it's hard to control, and it doesn't really give you a program that you can inspect, reuse, or compose.

What something like O1 is doing is closer to what I would call program search in natural language. The model is generating a chain of reasoning, evaluating it, backtracking, trying alternatives, and ultimately arriving at a sort of procedure that solves the problem. The model's weights stay fixed. What changes is the symbolic object it constructs at inference time. And to me that's closer to how I think intelligence actually works. You have a repertoire of reusable building blocks, and when you encounter a new situation, you search over combinations of those building blocks to synthesize a solution on the fly.

The appeal of that is it's much more aligned with the idea of intelligence as efficient skill acquisition. You're not re-learning your entire knowledge base for every new task. You're recombining what you already know in a targeted way, and the search process is where the generalization comes from. It's also much more scalable in terms of the kinds of problems you could handle, because the search can be deeper, it can be guided by the model's own intuition about which paths are promising, and the outputs are interpretable.

Now, to be clear, I think the ideal system is actually a merge of these two things. You want deep learning intuition to guide a discrete search process, and you probably also want some mechanism for the system to update its own building blocks as it accumulates experience, which is where something like test-time training or continual learning comes in. So it's not really either-or. But if you asked me which direction is closer to the core of what's missing in current systems, I would say it's the search and program synthesis side rather than just fine-tuning weights more aggressively.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would distinguish between adapting through search and adapting by updating your weights. With something like O1, you have a model that can generate a sequence of steps, explore possible solutions, and revise what it’s doing, all in the context of the current problem. That gives you a way to spend more computation on a problem without having to change the model itself.

Test-time training is also interesting, but you need a training signal. When you encounter a genuinely novel task, what exactly are you going to train on? You have a few examples, perhaps, but finding an objective that makes those updates improve your ability to solve the task is itself a difficult problem. You can easily adapt to superficial properties of the examples without acquiring the abstraction you actually need.

So my preference is for using a learned model to guide a search over solutions—or, ideally, over programs that explain the examples. The model supplies useful intuitions, and the search lets you construct something new for the situation you’re facing. That doesn’t mean an O1-style system has solved generalization, or that test-time training has no role. But I see guided search as a more direct way to turn additional computation into adaptation to a new problem.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would distinguish between adapting through a change in your weights and adapting through a computation that you run over your existing knowledge. With test-time training, you’re taking the new task and doing gradient descent on it. With an O1-like approach, you’re spending computation at inference time exploring possible solutions, checking intermediate steps, and revising what you’re doing.

I favor the second direction because a novel task often requires a new combination of things you already know. You don’t necessarily need to learn a new skill in your weights. You need to construct a program that solves this particular problem. And search gives you a way to do that while allocating more computation to harder problems.

That doesn’t mean test-time training is useless, or that O1 has solved this. The important question is what you’re searching over and how you recognize a good solution. But I think inference-time search is a more promising foundation for flexible adaptation than relying primarily on gradient updates.
